utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that it was impossible for the authorities to do anything in respect of the paramilitaries but you also testified that you were not a member of the government, you were no one special and you didn't take part in what was going on. Now, in contrast to you, the SJB was actively involved in events in municipality at the time and indeed they were tasked with maintaining law and order, so I'd like to look at what they said about the relationship between the paramilitaries and the government at that time. Could we please have P3390? And this time I'd like page 23 of the English and page 20 of the B/C/S. Now, Mr. Zelenovic, again, this is the SJB Zvornik annual report that you'll recall we looked at yesterday. And I'm interested in the passage beginning, "During July ...," and it states: "During July, the SJB personnel worked on carrying out their tasks stipulated by law. However the impact of the paramilitary formations could be felt at this time. The said formations had carried out their illegal activities with the knowledge and consent of some of the members of the temporary government of the municipality of Zvornik." And the document goes on to describe the problems the paramilitaries were causing, the check-points and the theft. And then it continues: "On the 27th of July, 1992, the police station personnel together with the military police expelled groups and individuals from the check-points and resumed control of the said locations. The reason for their action was that they were dissatisfied with the way they had been treated and with all the misuse on the part of the paramilitary and various members of the temporary government. The said members of the temporary government had, in fact, brought in the paramilitary units." So in fact, Mr. Zelenovic, according to the SJB at the time, members of the Zvornik civilian leadership brought in the paramilitaries, they were aware of their criminality and indeed they supported them in that criminality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My question is: It's correct, isn't it, that according to the SJB, the members of the Zvornik civilian leadership invited in the paramilitaries and supported them in their criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, there is more reference to the terror by the military -- paramilitary forces towards the legal forces. It boils down to exchanging accusations between the leadership and the others and to determine who actually had invited them. I, myself, cannot testify to any of this. These were all rumours and there are -- there is no accurate data about that and I'm not able to tell you anything more about it because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. I'll move on to one final topic. On paragraph -- in paragraph 34 of your statement, you say: "I am aware on the basis of what my fellow residents told me and on the basis of what I learned from the media, that all the arrested paramilitaries were brought to justice and convicted for their crimes and offences." Now, were you also aware that the paramilitaries who were arrested were then released shortly after their arrest?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, that's my knowledge, not from authentic sources, though, but what is most important in my view is that I no longer saw them in Zvornik. That would be my answer. It is possible that these things that you have just made reference to did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zelenovic, the then chief of the Zvornik SJB Marinko Vasilic recently testified before this Court that nothing was done to investigate the mass killings at either the Karakaj Technical School or Gero slaughterhouse. So --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me now is that the truth? Is that right? I think -- yes. Look, I think I'm not competent, and it's not my place to say whether those people were convicted or not. And I also on the other hand cannot deny what Mr. Vasilic has said. It's difficult to say anything about this issue after so many years and to confirm whether they were convicted or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two or three. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at page -- I'm sorry I failed to pause. At page 86, you were asked whether the local authorities supported Arkan and other groups, and you responded by saying that everyone was welcome to save you from terror. Can you tell us were the authorities supportive of the unlawful behaviour by Arkan and other groups?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full authority today that as far as the authorities from that time, with whom I was acquainted, did not support them but, rather, did their best and made every effort to - how shall I put it? - annihilate these paramilitaries from the municipality who, as I said, were not only for the authorities but to all citizens regardless of their ethnicities -- a tremendous problem and caused difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You wanted to say something about the photograph, and for that purpose could the witness please be shown P6413? Can you please tell us what it was that you wanted to say about respect to this photograph, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one photograph before this one, where the year was shown. Can we see that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be, then, 6412.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were two photographs and this was the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please have P6412?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, one can see here the year, but this is digit five which was cut in half. Madam Prosecutor said yesterday and I had to intervene and to repeat that because that was immediately after the unblocking of Zvornik. St. Archangel Michael is on the 21st of November and these events took place on the 8th of April, as far as I know, in 1992. So this is not right immediately. But it is definitely the year 1995 here, or the day when the Dayton Accords were signed, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So the war was over and the peace agreements were signed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, shall I ask the witness to read out the Cyrillic letters shown in the photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he read them out yesterday but he can read them out again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Patron Saint's Day, MUP, then you can't see that it says of Republika Srpska, St. Archangel Michael, Zvornik 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was interpreted properly because I'm looking at yesterday's transcript, [In English] saint, patron saint, patron saint. [Interpretation] In the Serbian tradition, it's Patron Saint's Day. And every institution can have its own patron saint. On yesterday's page 95, I'm going to read to you from line 13 to be quite clear, and I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "Well, all of these documents ... well, he had to cover these in financial terms, but this is how it arrived. I mean, on the basis of what I talked about then and when I asked them for help and what do I call them, these paramilitaries -- these paramilitaries threatened the factory." [Interpretation] Had you invited the paramilitary or did you appeal to the authorities because of the threats coming from the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say this. Every paper that I received at the time to review signed by the local president was not a proper document, if it was signed under coercion. However, these documents were signed under such circumstances due to the fact that those people were there on the spot. As far as the factory is concerned, I mentioned the example of the locomotive and the carriages that they were asking for, after which I agreed with my people to try and avoid this and give them a broken locomotive. Of course, as soon as they left the office, they were told this, he became angered and he wanted to take revenge on me. So we always, without exception, asked the authorities to keep them as far from the factory as possible, and this was the greatest damage that they caused to us. We had to give them a new locomotive that was operational and we, on our side, had to lease another one from the railways company and they did all kinds of things with this engine. And all the way through the 29th of July, when they were practically expelled from the municipality, we did our best to prevent them from coming there because we thought that it was not their place to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 91, of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested that there was a takeover of power in Zvornik. Who was the first to take over power in Zvornik and establish their authority in the town?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which side, the Muslim or the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after the lifting of the blockade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. Before the blockade. Who was it that blocked the town?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite a different thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I object to the line of questioning that I believe Mr. Karadzic is trying to get at. The scope of the cross-examination related simply to the -- what Mr. Zelenovic terms the lifting of the blockade and subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I tend to agree but I think Mr. Karadzic's re-examination is almost over. Yes, Mr. Robinson, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think Dr. Karadzic is reacting to the characterisation that the Prosecutor made of the takeover of the town of Zvornik, and the witness didn't actually react to that during the cross-examination so I think he's trying to clarify what was meant by takeover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, who controlled the town as of the 5th of April until the 10th, when the blockade was imposed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim forces. And as I said yesterday, in the meantime, Arkan came along, there were negotiations between the Muslim and Serbian sides in Mali Zvornik, that means in Serbia. Arkan came, beat up the Serbs in front of the Muslims, wanting in that manner to make a show of force or what -- I don't know, to compel or -- the other side to find a peaceful solution to these problems. However, whatever the Muslim side agreed and made promises to do under the pressure of the extremists who were practically imposing the blockade, ignored all of that, they chased them away and it came to nothing, and the outcome, as we know it, was inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say the extremists, whose extremists are you referring to, the ones that were preventing the finding of a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Muslim extremists of Zvornik who were practically in power and ruling Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 92, you said that the authorities called upon the civilians to come back. Did this call refer to Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably you can find it in various documents that this declaration applied to all citizens of Zvornik and in actual fact both ethnic community members started coming back. However, since Zvornik was crammed with paramilitary troops, practically violence continued against both sides, probably more against the Muslims than Serbs. I can say that I refrained from going back to Zvornik for two weeks for -- because of all this and especially because of my experience at the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my last question: After the unblocking, did the Serbian side took over control over the entire territory of Zvornik, and how many municipalities called Zvornik exist after the Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. This is outside the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond, we are talking about taking control over the municipality of Zvornik as a whole. Otherwise, I wouldn't have put that question and we all know that that was not the case. Even children know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, I think it's the same point. You told us to move on, but there -- as to who controlled Zvornik and who took it over, I think Dr. Karadzic has been trying to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, do I need to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, thank you. So, after these events, and practically until the end of war in 1995, the Serbian side controlled, but I cannot tell you exactly, 55 or 60 per cent of the territory of Zvornik municipality. And the remaining part was under the Muslim control, and that was the territory -- or the majority of territory was populated by Serbs. It's a huge area; for example, the place of Rastocnica. And I believe that in May 1992, all of this area was burnt down, the entire population was expelled, and this situation pertains to this very date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell me now how many municipalities of Zvornik do exist today and who they belong to?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR ZELENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are two of them. One is the Serbian municipality and the other is the Bosniak one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for your effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You're now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, I will deal with two matters regarding the MFI'd documents. First, the Chamber returns to the Prosecution's submission from Friday, 21st of June, 2013, regarding MFI P6394 and P6395, and notes that both documents were marked for identification on the 10th of June, 2013, pending the provision of English translations. The Chamber has reviewed the documents, their proposed translations and the relevant transcript excerpts and is satisfied that MFI P6394 and P6395 should now be marked as admitted. Next, in assessing the accused's motion to admit documents previously marked for identification filed on the 10th of June, 2013, the Chamber has noted issues with two of the documents tendered in the motion. First, regarding MFI D183, the Chamber notes that it contains significant portions which are illegible, rendering the English translation also incomplete. Second, a revised English translation for MFI D1720 has not been uploaded into e-court, as instructed by the Chamber in its decision of 7th December 2012. The Chamber therefore instructs the Defence, by Monday, 1st of July, 2013, to request and upload a revised translation for MFI D1720 and look into whether it has a more legible copy of D183 and, if so, to upload it into e-court along with a revised translation and to inform the Chamber of such. Please liaise with the Prosecution in locating a copy, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Grujic, probably you are already well aware of this, but before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have a request for you and I'm reminding myself at the same time. Let us speak slowly and clearly and let us pause between my questions and your answers because if we have to intervene, I mean if the interpreters intervene, then we are going to use up even more time. So please let us bear that in mind and you feel free to caution me too.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, have you provided a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D9681 in e-court? Thank you. We have the Serbian version. Please focus on the left-hand side of the screen. Do you see your statement there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was a bit too fast. Could you please pause.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said in your answers provided to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by each and every word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, here in the courtroom, would your answers basically be the same as those provided in this statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: They certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you with regard to the associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are nine associated exhibits on our witness list to be tendered. None of them are on our 65 ter list, so we would ask that they be added because we hadn't interviewed the witness at the time we filed that list. With respect to one of them, 1D15301 it's a photograph that bears some writing on it and we are going to lead that live so that the writing can be understood. With respect to the other eight associated exhibits we would ask that they be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any response to the Prosecution's concerning about some of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we hear from the Prosecution first? Yes, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, good morning. Yes, the Prosecution objects to the admission of 1D15311, 1D15314 and 1D15315 referenced in paragraph 45 of the statement for two reasons: First, they are not sufficiently discussed. They don't meet the standard for associated exhibits; and secondly, they consist of detailed evidence of crimes against Serbs and don't satisfy the standard of relevance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For 65 ter 18186 referred to in paragraph 53 is, first it's a document of a third -- is a -- that document is a third party statement, and the witness merely repeats the content of the statement without making any substantive comment. So the Chamber is not minded to admit those four exhibits as an associated exhibit. In order for the Defence to tender them the Defence should lead them live as well as showing the relevance of those documents, if it so wishes. So we'll admit the four associated exhibits, i.e., 1D7326, 7442, 7443 and 7444. Shall we assign the numbers, first to the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, statement document 1D9681 receives number D3724.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And four other associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receive number D3725, D3726, D3727 and D3728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language the summary of Mr. Branko Grujic's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Branko Grujic was a member of the SDS since its formation and was elected the first president of the SDS municipal board in Zvornik on 1st September -- of September 1990. After the first multi-party elections, the government was formed, local governments functioned normally for half a year. In mid-1991 the coalition agreement was violated by the SDA leaders in Zvornik. The violation included obstructions and outvoting in the local assembly by SDA politicians so that any agreement aimed at normalising relations was rejected from the outset by Muslims. They appointed people without agreement. Some who were unqualified to manage position in public enterprises. All SDS efforts and objections to reach an agreement were met with objection and the blockage of normal political activity. Mr. Branko Grujic initiated a number of discussions with leading Muslims from the SDA. The SDA in Zvornik had received instructions from the SDA headquarters in Sarajevo to operate politically in this way. The aim was to install loyal Muslims and SDA personnel in important positions in Zvornik, to strengthen their activity within the entire Muslim body in Zvornik municipality. Asim Jusubasic told Branko Grujic he did not agree with what was coming from Sarajevo but they were monitoring him, where his own Muslim colleagues were monitoring him and he had to do what was ordered. Alija Izetbegovic had already conceptualised all of this in his Islamic Declaration, stating that the time had come to put it into action. The situation in Zvornik worsened after 15th of October, 1991, when the rump Presidency of BH without the Serbs ordered that federal laws no longer be complied with, that recruits and reservists were not to be sent to the JNA, that financial transactions be blocked and that BH move to independence be accelerated. The Patriotic League was formed in Zvornik at the beginning of 1991. And Muslim soldiers formed the ranks in Godus village, the Zvornik SDA placed their personnel in leading position in the police in Zvornik, without SDS consents and began forming a Muslim police force. Serbs in Zvornik were helpless to do anything to prevent the formation of mono-ethnic Muslim armed units. Interethnic relations between Muslims and Serbs in Zvornik were badly damaged by mid-1991. Several incidents occurred in Zvornik, including older Serbs dressed in folk clothing being attacked, Serb women selling their wares being abused and physically assaulted on JNA officer in Zvornik. The Handzar Division was manned exclusively by Muslims and committed many crimes against the Serbs in Podrinje and Zvornik. There was no one to complain to about the incident because the police was led by Muslim criminals, and Muslims in surrounding villages were well-armed and almost every night they would come to the outskirts of Serbian villages and open fire. All of these activities were co-ordinated by Asim Alic, a Muslim sent from Sarajevo pursuant to a directive from SDA leaders. These caused fear and anxiety amongst the Serbs. The Serbian policemen who worked at the station at that time were not allowed to go on patrol in Muslim villages. Conscious of the situation and with the aim of finding a solution to this situation according to the directive from President Karadzic, the SDS would be persistent in holding talks and reaching agreements and that conflicts should be avoided a joint initiative of the SDA and SDS was given -- SDS was given, asking everyone to respect each other as neighbours and overcome problems. The Muslims responded to all calls for talks but they did not respect any agreements. The Crisis Staff was formed within the Zvornik SDS. The basic focus on the Crisis Staff -- of the Crisis Staff was to establish contacts with the leaders of the Muslims and begin negotiations, all with the aim of normalising the situation and preventing further victims. The Muslims in Zvornik were under great pressure from Muslims in Tuzla and Sarajevo and were -- there was much talk of the -- of Bosnia becoming Muslim. On 3rd and 4th of April, 1992, road and settlements in Zvornik were blocked by armed members of the Patriotic League and the Muslim part of MUP. The next day, the Patriotic League ambushed and opened fire on a JNA vehicle, killing a JNA officer and wounding a number of soldiers. This attack in Sapna was planned by the Muslims and it was a signal for an all-out Muslim attack on Serbs in Zvornik. News quickly spread and many Serbs and some Muslims fled Zvornik. Fear reigned among the Serbs and the possibility of a reoccurrence of the Second World War and heavily armed Muslim formations arrived from Tuzla and Sarajevo to aid the Muslims in Zvornik. Conscious of the situation in which Muslim extremists controlled the town, Branko Grujic sought to prevent the mass slaughter of the Serbs by starting negotiations with Muslim leaders in Zvornik. On April the 6th, 1992, Arkan and Peja assumed full control of the situation. Arkan personally continued negotiating with the Muslims. Serbs in Zvornik no longer had any authority and all the power was in the hands of Arkan. After the blockade of Zvornik was lifted, Arkan left the area but individuals from his unit remained and formed paramilitary group for the purpose of looting and carrying out criminal acts. Serbs and Muslims became hostages and victims of their criminal acts. The local government had absolutely no influence on the paramilitaries. They made all the decisions. Policemen in uniform were frequently abused. Branko Grujic and Marinko Vasilic secretly went to Pale to inform President Karadzic about the problems in Zvornik. He was visibly surprised and astonished by the news. He said he would undertake every measure and activity for the gang to be arrested. On 29th of July, 1992, strong police forces from the MUP of RS in co-ordinated action with the units of military police entered Zvornik using force and arrested the paramilitaries. President Karadzic always requested that about Branko Grujic hold talks and seek agreements for peaceful solutions to problems in Zvornik. He wanted maximum efforts to find a peaceful solution to problems and conflicts with the aim of avoiding any conflict. And that would be the short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could call up that photo, 1D15301.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, you were very kind, and I should like to thank you for that. I mean for this photograph. Did you bring us this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who took this photograph and what is written there? What does it represent?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken during my trial in Belgrade. Already in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, could you speak a bit more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters? Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My people from my defence and my sons brought this to me when I was tried in Belgrade. It was brought as evidence that the Muslim side already in 1991, that is to say almost half a year before the war started and any kind of commotion in Bosnia, the Muslim side publicly lined up an armed unit fully armed in uniform with slogans that amounted to threats against the Serbs, saying that there was no place for them in Bosnia any longer, that their country was Serbia and that they should go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the transcript, and for the participants, could you slowly read what is written on this board?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: This is what they say here. This is where --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please start from the beginning, from the top.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: "Welcome in Godus," and then it says, "the first organised resistance to the aggressor." So we were aggressors already in 1991 until no rifles had been fired. Whose aggressors were we? Were we aggressors against our own homes, our own properties, our own families?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, did you know that they were being lined up and that they were armed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: We knew straight away. We were informed by our people who happened to be passing by and who took this picture and saw that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just read the date when this took place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: The 17th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This lineup, this lineup, when did that happen? That is not reflected in the transcript. How did this reflect on the situation and how did people feel especially the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: There was astonishment all over. War was raging in Croatia and it became clear that it would spill over into Bosnia because if somebody comes out openly with a rifle, lines up and makes speeches based on ethnic hatred, what else could we expect? We could only expect that the next thing would be a campaign against the Serb people, against Serb houses, against Serb children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, where is Godus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Godus is 20 something kilometres away from Zvornik towards Lopare, up there. From Sapna, about 7, 8 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D15301 receives number D3729, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I shall give up on the other exhibits. And at this moment, I have no further questions for Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Grujic, as you have noted now, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in most part admitted in writing, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before I begin, if I could clarify, as Your Honours noted 65 ter 1D186 in paragraph 53 -- paragraph 53 really, as Your Honour said, the witness merely repeats the content of the statement without making any substantive comment. So if this document is not being tendered I'm wondering if paragraph 53 of the statement should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view the paragraph can stand on its own. Shall we continue? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You have given a tape recorded interview to the Prosecution, you recall that, in 2002. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also gave evidence in your own trial against you and Mr. Popovic at the beginning of that trial in 2005; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 15 of your statement, you refer to a joint declaration signed by you and Asim Jusubasic. It's been admitted as D3725 and you assert in your statement that this was part of your efforts to reach a peaceful solution. Now, that declaration says, among other things, "Let us do everything not to seek weapons." But, in fact, Mr. Grujic, before the war, you yourself were personally involved in arming Serbs in Zvornik through the SDS structures. You told the OTP that in 2002, and it's true; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That did happen. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not interpret it that way, "that did happen." The witness said, "bilo je toga." It would have been better to say "there had been things like that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Grujic, you as the head of the SDS municipal board received arms and you distributed them to the local SDS boards in Zvornik. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No, that is not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 25264, please? This is a transcript of the interview the witness gave to the OTP in 2002 and just I'd like to inform everyone in the courtroom that the English has been transcribed and we have some of the B/C/S also transcribed, but I'd just like to point out that it's not a translation that the English parts were transcribed and then separately some of the B/C/S was transcribed so they don't always match entirely, in particular some of what Mr. Grujic said was not picked up by the audio so there are some parts in the B/C/S that are inaudible but they are audible in the English. If we could go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Gustafson, you asked the witness whether he testified in the trial of Mr. Popovic in 2005? What case did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, that was his own case against -- it was the trial against himself and Mr. Popovic jointly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 58 of the English and page 57 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, this is a transcript of the interview you gave to the OTP in 2002. And this is page 58 of the English. Yes. Okay, so in the middle of the page in the English towards the bottom in the B/C/S, you're asked: "What was the role of the SDS in arming the Serbs?" And you answer: "One of the supply lines, to put it in this way, went through Marko Pavlovic who was connected with Mr. Spasojevic who sent a certain amount of arms over and these arms were distributed through the SDS local boards. As they were staying in Slavonia and Baranja where war was already going on, the arms was collected and this is how it was." If we go to the next page in the B/C/S, you're asked: "What role did you have in that?" And you said: "We have this board of ours and when we received arms we would just -- we distributed a couple of these items to our local boards. That was in late 1991, towards the end of 1991." And then you're asked: "How many weapons and what type of weapons were distributed through the SDS in 1991 and the beginning of 1992?" You answer: "I don't know exactly but I know it was old Thompson 81 and the old outdated rifles M48 which were impossible to sell even on the black market." And you're asked again: "But how many weapons are we talking about? Are we talking 10 or 10.000?" And you say: "Well, 10.000 would be too much, we didn't even have that many -- much soldiers. It was rather a couple hundred items, and there might have been a situation in which somebody else received the weapons and distributed them subsequently. What I know about is that a couple of hundred items reached us and we have distributed them further on." Mr. Grujic, you told the OTP in 2002 that the SDS municipal board received weapons through Marko Pavlovic and Dragan Spasojevic, and you distributed them to the SDS local boards; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down while reading? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One person from SDS took part in all of this and that is Dragan Spasojevic who was at that time the commander of the police station, and who somehow got in touch with some man from Baranja, his name was Rade, something like that, I'm not quite sure, who sent him to Marko Pavlovic's address, who was our commander later, and they agreed together and brought in a small quantity of about a thousand -- a hundred pieces of old type weapons, Thompsons, some old fashioned 48s, which were some 50 or 60 years old, from the previous war, and they distributed that near Dragan's house to people. Dragan intended them for and whom he picked. And I was informed that this was done by Dragan and distributed. I can say that at that time, it was general hysteria about weapons after this unit was lined up. Everybody wanted to buy anything. I bought something for myself on the black market. I paid a small calibre rifle, 1800 German marks. And if there was any sort of distribution of weapons I would definitely have taken one for myself. I wouldn't have bought a weapon for myself and given it to the others because then later when the distribution of weaponry occurred, the bad weapons were distributed, so the SDS had a minimal or no role in that. Dragan, as the police commander, together with Marko Pavlovic, distributed that small quantity, just in case so that each village could protect itself, at least a little bit, if there was an attack on the village so that they could repel the attack and protect the Serbian population, the Serbian women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. I'm going to ask you to try to keep your answers focused on the specific question that I ask. You referred to Dragan Spasojevic's contact in this arming activity who put him in touch with Marko Pavlovic as someone by the name of Rade. That was Rade Kostic; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender these portions of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not translated, the witness did not get the interpretation whether it was Rade Kostic only Rade was said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, later I realised it's Rade Kostic. I first managed to remember just the first name but then I remembered that it is Rade Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the page numbers again, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes it's pages 58 and 59 in the English and 57 and 58 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P6414, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, you said also in your statement that you only learned in court and that I presume is a reference to your own trial that Marko Pavlovic's real name was Branko Popovic and that he had been brought to Zvornik by the Zvornik SJB commander Dragan Spasojevic. But in fact, you told the OTP back in 2002 that it was Dragan Spasojevic who introduced to you Marko Pavlovic in 1991, and in 2002 you told the OTP that Marko Pavlovic was also known as Branko Popovic. So you were aware of these facts in 2002 long before your own trial; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No. Wrong. You did not understand me correctly. I met Marko Pavlovic with Dragan Spasojevic at the Jezera hotel in Mali Zvornik a couple of months before the war broke out and he was introduced to me as Marko Pavlovic, and I contacted that person throughout the whole war and only later, after the war, when this investigation was initiated, I found out from The Hague investigators what his real name was. Until The Hague investigators came, I did not know his real name, and believe me, even to this day I don't believe that's that because for years I operated on the premise that his name was Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you what you said to the OTP in a moment but first I'll ask you one more question about Pavlovic. In your statement you said that Pavlovic presented himself to you as an officer with strong ties to the JNA but you later learned that you were deceived and Marko Pavlic -- Pavlovic was actually Branko Popovic someone who knew Arkan. And again you told the OTP in 2002 that were you aware from the very beginning that Marko Pavlovic was a close friend of Arkan's because you could see that with your own eyes at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: When Arkan came to Zvornik, after a certain amount of time, Marko Pavlovic popped up as well. I could see that they knew each other, they greeted each other, they talked, and there was a close relationship between them, so I got the impression that they knew each other. I was convinced that they knew each other. And as for whether I knew that he was Branko Popovic or not, well, you can believe me that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you -- as I said, you say in your statement that Marko Pavlovic presented himself to you as an officer with strong ties to the JNA but when you met Pavlovic, when Dragan Spasojevic introduced him to you, Dragan Spasojevic told you that it was Rade Kostic, a MUP operative who had introduced Marko Pavlovic to Spasojevic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said a few moments ago that when Arkan came to Zvornik after a certain amount of time Marko Pavlovic popped up as well. But it's correct, isn't it, that Marko Pavlovic attended a number of Zvornik Crisis Staff meetings and advised you on how to organise yourselves? You said that in your own trial and that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Marko would come and join us at our meetings from time to time. He asked about the situation, what it was like, were there any problems, were there any incidents, and often he would advise as to how to it resolve some problem, mostly it would always be advice to proceed as peacefully as possible, to resolve everything with negotiations, agreement, peacefully, and then sometimes if something had to be done at our detriment, it would -- it should be, it ought to be done only in a peaceful way in order to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you haven't said anything in your statement or in your testimony so far about how Arkan came to arrive in Zvornik but in 2002 you told the OTP that Dragan Spasojevic, the Zvornik SJB commander and Crisis Staff member brought Arkan to Zvornik and that Spasojevic informed you in advance that Arkan would be coming; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: A part of what you say is correct. Spasojevic appeared together with Arkan at the door of the Crisis Staff on the 6th of April at about 10.00 approximately, and as soon as Arkan entered the room where the Crisis Staff was located, he asked, Who is the president of the Crisis Staff here? I said, That's me. He replied, Not any more. You have been replaced. It's now Dragan Spasojevic. And from that point on, they took over, conducted meetings, agreed on further plans, everything else was something that they later planned and executed, the two of them, and I had the impression that Spasojevic was not asked about anything either, simply Arkan took everything in his own hands and he commanded everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you told the OTP that Arkan and his men arrived in Zvornik in vehicles with either federal MUP or Serbian MUP licence plates; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to -- because your answer is not that clear, I'm going to ask you again, Mr. Grujic: You told the OTP that Dragan Spasojevic told you in advance that Arkan would be coming to Zvornik. Do you accept that that -- or do you deny it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No. He did not say that to me. It must be a bad translation, if that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 68 in both languages in this document, this is near the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and the middle in the English, and you were asked about Arkan, "Were you advised that he was coming to Zvornik?" And you say, "No, but once I was advised by Dragan that he got in touch with Arkan and that there is a possibility of his arrival in Zvornik," and if we go to the next page in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be read in the Serbian the way it sounds and could the interpreters please translate?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the witness can read along. This is at -- this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's important to read along with the transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then you were asked, "When was that?" And you answered, "Just before the conference," but I understand that that should read "conflict" in the B/C/S, "immediately after Bijeljina, I don't know where that occurred," and you're asked, "Was it -- it was between the attack on Bijeljina and his arrival in Zvornik; is that correct?" And you say, "Yes, exactly." And in the next page of the English, you were asked, "Do you know why he was supposed to be coming to Zvornik?" And you answer, "Dragan just said -- Dragan said Arkan will be coming to Zvornik and then he arrived indeed and it was like this." So Mr. Grujic, you made it quite clear to the OTP in 2002 that Dragan Spasojevic advised you in advance that Arkan would be coming to Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Not correct. I already said that he arrived suddenly at the door of the room where we were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, it's a catastrophe with the translations. They are incorrect and malicious and tendentious. Nowhere in the English version is it indicated that anything was unclear, whereas the Serbian version is full of unclear things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I thought I explained that. The interview was being simultaneously interpreted, and the witness's -- and Mr. Karadzic is welcome to review the audio tape and he will confirm this because I have -- the witness's remarks are largely or many of them are inaudible but the -- the interpreter's translation of the witness's remarks are much clearer, and that is why there is a difference between what is transcribed in B/C/S and what is transcribed in English. There is nothing malicious about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. How is this B/C/S version prepared? Is it another translation of English version or is a transcription of the audio taped?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Exactly. It's the transcription of the B/C/S of this interview which was being simultaneously -- not simultaneously consecutively interpreted by an interpreter. So what was said in English is in the English transcript and what was said in B/C/S is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is: Is this B/C/S version is a transcription of B/C/S words or the translation of English transcription?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: A transcription of B/C/S words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then which could be checked against the audio tape recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They can both be checked against the audio because all the English and all the B/C/S is present in the audio. It's just that the B/C/S -- what -- what the witness himself said in the B/C/S is difficult to make out in the audio in many places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now where are we? He answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd like to tender -- add these two pages to P6414, it's 68 and 69 of the English and of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: B/C/S page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The same, 68 and 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll add them. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, this is really unacceptable. We cannot -- we can hear what Mr. Grujic says in the Serbian, on the tape, and we can hear how that is being translated but we cannot check whether it was actually interpreted correctly. What is transcribed in Serbian is something that the witness would need to read and then our translators here could translate it because the sense, the meaning, has been changed. We don't know who the interpreter was, why he embroidered and added to the sentences. Simply in that way this cannot be sneaked into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like ask the president if I can explain. I had a lot of problems at the trial in Belgrade as well with this statement because there are many things that are mistranslated here or are not translated the way they were said. So I would like you to keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard the explanation from Ms. Gustafson and let us proceed on that basis, and if you have some specific problem you can raise it. There are many ways for you to deal with it, but in the meantime, let us proceed. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make sure that you show the relevant B/C/S page to the witness as well as to the interpreters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic I would like to turn to another topic now. At paragraph 18 of your statement, you state that the SDS leadership issued instructions, and based on those instructions you formed an SDS Crisis Staff on the 22nd of December, 1991. Those instructions you refer to, those are the Variant A and B instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in late December, I received a notification from the SDS HQ which I considered to be some kind of instruction that could possibly serve in our conditions, so that we could use some of that also and do something on the basis of that because we were not in a better situation to do something better. So we accepted that, to a degree we acted upon some of the instructions, some of the parts, and to another extent in keeping with the situation in our municipality, we adapted and behaved the way we had to behave.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you testified in your own case, you stated that you considered the Variant A and B instructions to have emanated directly from Dr. Karadzic and that were you obliged to implement them. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I said to an extent, only partially, because we used what we could adapt in our particular conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, we are hearing many times that Mr. Grujic was tried and testified. Does his statement contain some introductory part about his trial? Does it mention about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President. I have to look at that more careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Otherwise probably you may let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, the statement doesn't mention it. I intend to get into it in my cross-examination. If we could have 65 ter 24648, which is Mr. Grujic's testimony in his own trial. And I'd like in particular page 45 of the English and page 32 of the B/C/S. And it's at the very bottom of the page in the B/C/S, the very last thing that you're recorded as saying. It's also at the bottom in the English. If we could scroll to the very bottom in the B/C/S, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it says -- you say: "On the 20-something December we also received this instruction, Variants A and B. If you've read that, this was sometime around the 20th, so in five, six days' time we proceeded according to that instruction and we formed the Serb Municipality of Zvornik." If we could turn the page in the B/C/S: "That is to say we elected a president, elected all the organs, adopted enactments of the Serb Municipality of Zvornik which was tasked with being in readiness in case it came to clashes, in case it came to dissent, so that we have our own organs, that we pulled out to the Serb territory and that we function independently there, so as to organise our Serb people as best as possible and in order to protect it as best as possible." Then this is on the next page in the English, I'm sorry, and the judge asked you: "What function were you given in this division of power?" And you ask [sic]: "According to the instruction." And the judge says: "According to instruction A and B." And you answer: "Radovan wrote that the president of the municipal board was the president of the Crisis Staff too. You could read this there." I'd like to show you another passage where you discuss these instructions at page 161 of the English and 108 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, why don't you break down your question? If you like, the witness to answer simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's quite a simple question. It's just that he said -- he made a few different comments about it. My question at the end of showing him what he said before is quite straightforward. I'm -- I can try to break it up if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, that's what you said in your trial, right, that you considered these instructions to have emanated directly from Radovan Karadzic's pen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: This came from the SDS HQ which also had its own professional services that drafted the materials. I don't know whether Radovan is directly involved in that or not. Whether he knew about it or not is something that I really could not know having been in Zvornik but I received it from the central, and I believed that it should have been applied depending on the situation. Our municipality had a lot of Serbian population and there was a need because we could see war was getting prepared so we made a decision, we formed the organs, so that in case a conflict broke out, it would make it possible for us to initiate those organs immediately in order to prevent anarchy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The municipality had a Serbian minority.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. I cut you off because you were moving away from my specific question. If we could go to page 161 of the English and 108 of the B/C/S. And here, in the middle of both pages in -- you give a relatively long answer and about halfway through that answer, you say, they suggested at meeting of the Main Board which I was not a member of, Jovo Mijatovic was a member of that Main Board, they suggested creating an instruction for operating in extraordinary circumstances if such extraordinary circumstances should arise, you see. And then Radovan, and I don't know who, their expert team wrote an instruction saying this is how to act in municipalities with Serbian majority and this is how to act in municipalities with a Serbian minority. Now, you just said I don't know whether Radovan was directly involved in that or not but this is another reflection from your prior testimony that you considered Variant A and B instructions to have come directly from Radovan Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 162 and the next page in English and the next page in the B/C/S? And this is near the top in the English and at the very top in the B/C/S, you say: "Under the Variant B, where the Serbs were in minority, we were obliged to form a Crisis Staff, elect a parallel Serbian assembly which would come out to the Serbian territory and immediately form a government the moment the conflict breaks out," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the "i tako dalje," "and so on and so forth," be also read out?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, this passage reflects your view that the Variant A and B instructions were mandatory, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I already explained that. I considered this as a principled direction or instruction that ought to have been applied to the extent that it applied to the given situation in the municipality. All the municipalities had a different situation, municipalities with a majority Serb population did not have to do anything. Municipalities that were half and half had a different situation, and the municipalities with smaller quantity of Serbian citizens had a different way and different conditions and a different situation, and they had to act according to the conditions that prevailed and to the situation that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender these passages. It was page 45, 46, 161 and 162 of the English and 32 and 33, 108 and 109 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them. Shall we assign the number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number would be P6415, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break if it is convenient, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It is. Thank you. I didn't notice the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic in your statement at paragraph 18 you said after you received the Variant and A and B instructions that the republican organs "did not control us or ask about its implementation." But you told the OTP in the 2002 that the Crisis Staff in Zvornik would report back to the republic level and receive and implement additional republic-level instructions. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik, we heard Deputy Jovo Mijatovic who was the president of the Executive Board of the party who attended our meetings and he was our main source of information, and in turn, we tasked him with conveying all our conclusions and decisions from our meetings to the appropriate levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Similarly, he would convey instructions from the republic level to the Zvornik Crisis Staff for implementation; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you about one republic level instruction that you personally received just before the outbreak of the conflict, if we could go to 65 ter 25264, page 165 of the English and page 79, the B/C/S, and this relates to your claim at paragraph 44 of your statement that in all your direct contacts with Dr. Karadzic, he always requested that you hold talks and seek agreement for a peaceful solution. And here you told the investigators: So I remember a meeting that was held in Pale immediately prior to the eruption of the conflict when Radovan invited presidents of the municipalities, municipal boards, different MPs, also members of the executive boards, et cetera. It was a very extended meeting. To the best of my recollection it was held sometime after the 20th of March, before the assembly. And the usual agenda was discussed towards the end of the meeting, toward midnight. Radovan told us, "Gentlemen, the conflict will probably erupt." And that it would be very soon. He told us that it was up to us that were present there to accept the conflict and that the first task, in case of the conflict, was to protect our people, whereas the second task was to create Serbian territories where Serbs were in majority, to create some kind of cantons or areas with Serb population in majority. Then Radovan told us when we did our best to complete these tasks, when we protected our people and protected our territories, we had to be ready to be actually exposed to a very ungrateful attitude by our own people and they might spit at us, meaning they will be very ungrateful for what we did for them. Who was capable of doing this and who was ready for such sequence of events should stay here. Whoever is not ready to accept it should leave right now. Then I remember the three people left, they said, "We are unwilling to accept this kind of development." Everybody else remained, and then he took a look at us and asked us if we are aware of what we had to do and we are aware that we would be betrayed by our own people and they would be unpleased by what we did for them. Now, this is true, isn't it, Mr. Grujic? You along with a large group of SDS officials attended this meeting sometime in late March prior to an assembly session and received these instructions from Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: This is a lot to do with poor translation. However, this is basically what I said, that is that President Karadzic, and he unlined it many times, that in the municipalities that the Serbs have power and are in majority, all other ethnic communities should even enjoy an advantageous position and not be oppressed in any way. We have to be different, we should even try to ingratiate ourselves to other nationalities, we had to prove that we were good people and that we are well-wishers and that we want to do good for them. Since Dr. Karadzic, our president, is a psychologist, he evaluated the situation properly and he told us the right thing, which is that whatever and however much our people do, we cannot satisfy everybody because it is our common practice to criticise every previous leadership and that happened on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, the interpretation is completely different. Line 2 on page 40, I'm going to read what I said. It says, "Do you know what I told you?" In other words, you have to do your best and your people will eventually -- I didn't ask you what you had to do but what I told you. Line 2 was wrongly interpreted. No, I'm sorry, wrongly recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that there is mistranslation. Quite a lot of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Grujic you had an opportunity to read along what you actually said during your interview in the B/C/S. Can you point to any specific passage that you claim was mistranslated?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: In the part of my statement given to the OTP interrogators or, rather in the whole of it, there was so many mistranslations that it was nearly unusable and futile and it went to such an extent that I suspect it to be malevolent. I don't know if it was a bad translator who didn't know his or her job or whether it was done intentionally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, this same sentence was erroneously translated in the English version, Ms. Gustafson read it correctly but the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness about this very topic so I'd like to ask the accused not to intervene on this at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, do you understand that the text on the left-hand side of your screen is a transcription of your words in your language during the OTP interview? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Look, there are places where it says, unintelligible which means that was a poor recording. Lots of things have been either omitted or badly translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Or were simply inaudible on the audio tape; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, how would he know that? He hasn't listened to the audio tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How would he know that things have been either omitted or badly translated either, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the B/C/S version, which we see on the left side, is not a translation. Is it direct transcription from the audio recording as far as it is audible?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are many reasons for not being able to hear the part, overlapping or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, do you recall thanking the OTP at the end of this interview for "fair treatment, cultured conversation, and good co-operation? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but that was just a display of courtesy on my part because the gentlemen were at times quite rude to me, not to say brazen, which made me at one point bang my fist on the table and say, I'm not going to do this any longer, you should behave as human beings otherwise I'm suspending the -- their boss intervened, he changed the collocutor, and the conversation continued in a different tone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender these pages, pages 165 of the English and page 79 of the B/C/S. I'd like to add them to P6414, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them to P6414.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask for a revision of the translation to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to take the steps for the revision of the translation in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, in your statement you make a number of assertions about alleged aggressive and threatening activities carried out by the Muslim side in the period leading up to the takeover on the 9th of April. For example, at paragraph 13 you talk about the elderly Serbs in Zvornik town being attacked, you talk about Muslims opening fire on Serbian villages in paragraph 14, and then at paragraph 29 you say that when the Muslims blocked the town on the 6th of April they searched Serb homes and physically abused Serbs in the town, and that people were fleeing Zvornik, Serbs were fleeing Zvornik to escape this mistreatment. But when you testified in your own trial, you were asked if there was any shooting, arrest, torture and exile of the Serbs before Arkan proclaimed the liberation of Zvornik and you said there were no tortures or exiles, only the atmosphere of -- was such that people were afraid and ran away and that atmosphere was arming and training activities by the Muslims. And that's correct, isn't it? It was the arming and training activities by the Muslim side that caused the Serbs to be afraid; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Not only training. There was shooting as well, over the Serb villages. So let me say it's -- it instilled fear in the Serbian villagers, even my house was targeted, it's located in a valley and one evening somebody fired a burst of fire with flares and I immediately called Asim Jusubasic, the president of the SDA, and he said, I'm going to check this and I'll get back to you, and, indeed, some ten minutes later he called me back and said it is true but this will not repeat again. So not only that the villages were targeted, specific leaders were targeted as well, in order to slow down their activities and their preparations for the defence of their people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, personal computer. LiveNote in personal computer does not work. Probably we need to restart but we can follow from the public monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic in your statement you said that the Zvornik Crisis Staff only became operational on the 6th of April, 1992. The Trial Chamber has received in evidence an order you issued as Crisis Staff commander on the 5th of April ordering a trial mobilisation of all TO units in the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik. That's P5505. And indeed you testified in your own case that this order was carried out, a count of manpower was taken and as a result of that count, you had 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, you haven't read this order to the end. That was not a mobilisation order. It was a trial mobilisation order because in those days, after Mustafic distributed weapons one evening to the worst criminals and allowed them to walk like that around the town, which caused the Serbian people to become frightened and to flee to Serbia en masse together with their women and children, seeking shelter in Serbia. But it's not only the Serbs, the Muslims as well, and a large number of them fled and crossed over to Serbia which means that there was an overwhelming fear and the sense of uncertainty and there were rumours that a lot of able bodied Serbs had also fled to Serbia and in order for me to check that without waiting for the conflict to erupt, which seemed inevitable, I had to issue an order on trial mobilisation in order to find out the level of manpower with whom I'm going to face the enemy and defend the Serbian villages and Serbian people and for that reason I issued such an order without waiting for a decision of the Crisis Staff. I did it on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 44, line 22, the witness said the night before that the weapons were distributed, "not one evening," but the night before the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Grujic, that order was implemented, a count was taken, and as a result you had 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers. You became aware of that fact; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: After I -- visiting all the villages and after obtaining some information, I established that only a few people fled, so the information that many people had fled to Serbia was not correct. All of them or nearly all of them remained to defend their family homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that amounted to 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely because I don't know what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you. If we could have P -- sorry, 65 ter 24648. If we could have page 52 in the English and page 37 in the B/C/S. This is right around the middle of the page in the B/C/S, it's towards the bottom in the English, and you're asked when the decision on mobilisation was taken and you say the decision on mobilisation was the first test, the decision was taken on the 5th of April. And if we could go to the next page in the English, and towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, this is at the middle of the English, you were asked how many men fit for military service were there? Did you take a count? And you answered there were 90 per cent of all those who were otherwise then in the municipality, and you were asked how many that was in terms of numbers, and you said you didn't know precisely and you said once we organised ourselves we had approximately 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers. And the judge says when was this when you organised yourselves fully, was that on the 8th of April or when?
