And then you answered that was approximately on the 5th when we called the troop review on the 6th. Does that remind you, Mr. Grujic, that when you [indiscernible] this trial mobilisation, you became aware that you had 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers in the municipality? In the TO, I should say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: There is no dispute about that but I cannot guarantee the number. I may have said exactly that figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, if I could add these pages to P6415, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grujic, you also testified in your own case that at the beginning of April, a separate Serbian MUP in Zvornik was established in Karakaj in the Alhos building pursuant to Momcilo Mandic's dispatch ordering the Serb police to separate. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the dispatch. We made our own agreement that our policemen must not remain in the station that was manned majority by the Muslims because even before that they had been prohibited from visiting and patrolling the Muslim villages and that was done by the then chief, and of course we agreed as a Crisis Staff that we would take with us and pull out all the Serbian organs that had been set up pursuant to an assembly decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 73 of the English and page 50 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a short break in light of the technical difficulties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a ten-minute break. --- Break taken at 11.31 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, you just finished testifying that you weren't aware of Momcilo Mandic's dispatch ordering the Serb police to separate and I'd like to direct your attention to the very bottom of this page of your previous testimony, and this is also towards the bottom in the B/C/S, where you say, towards the end of a rather long answer: "The only thing that was established immediately at the beginning, I know, was the Ministry of the Interior. And it started operating immediately already on 4 April, 3 April, pardon me, the deputy minister sent a dispatch to the SUP for the Serb police to separate from --" And the Presiding Judge interrupts you and says: "Was that where when they well to Alhos there to Karakaj?" And you said: "Yes, yes." And the judge asked: "The MUP?" And you said: "Yes." So contrary to what you said a moment ago, you were not only aware of Momcilo Mandic's dispatch but testified that that is what caused the police to separate and move to Alhos; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No. I did not know about this dispatch. Quite accidentally, we separated it after what happened in Zvornik, but later on I found out that there was a dispatch but when we carried out the separation I did not know that it existed. The dispatch arrived on the 4th and we learned only one or two days later so we did not know on the 4th, we found out only on the 5th or 6th, actually, on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, this testimony indicates that what you found out later on was that the Zvornik Serbian MUP separated pursuant to Momcilo Mandic's dispatch. That's what you learned later; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: We learned later that there was a dispatch too, but, yes, and we carried out the separation without knowing about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page. I'd like to add it to P6415, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grujic, at paragraph 55 of your statement, you said that you did not invite any paramilitary forces to Zvornik. But whether or not you specifically invited a specific group or groups to Zvornik, what is true is that you, and by you I mean the municipal authorities, announced over the radio that you needed men and then the volunteers arrived, they reported to the TO headquarters, and from there they were assigned, and that's what you said in your trial, and that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: After the de-blockade of Zvornik, we announced, and said that those who wanted to help us should come and they would be welcome. However, before the de-blockade, no one had any contact with volunteers and no one called anyone. Arkan came at his own initiative together with Mr. Spasojevic to the Crisis Staff, I don't know now whether someone told Spasojevic, Go and call Arkan, or whether Arkan came on his own and reported directors of the police. I wouldn't want to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to read a few comment you made in your own trial about your attitude towards the arrival of these groups. So you testified that you [indiscernible] Zuca on the 8th of April in Karakaj headquarters and you did not ask who he was because "why would I ask? Whoever comes comes voluntarily. Trust me, people, that person is welcome." That's page 76. You were asked whether you inquired where the volunteers were from and you said, "Well, what would I be inquiring for? Any volunteer's arrival was good for us." And you were asked whether you were interested in where they came from, you said, "No I was not. I saw a Serb man who had come to help the Serb people. That was it, that was enough for me." That's page 92. Do those statements accurately reflect your attitude towards the arrival of the paramilitary units to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: We were a municipality with a minority Serb population. That is to say that we were under threat in terms of the military power that the opponents had and that we had, and every person who came to help us was welcome. We were really happy to see everyone who came. And I thank on this day as well those who were honourable and honest and who came to help us. It is true that I did not ask who you were and where you came from, I just said welcome. And over there you should go to the headquarters, to the command, and you should be deployed and go and protect our people. That was our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you claim you had no influence on the paramilitary groups, that you were at the mercy of these groups and that your lives were endangered; for example, at paragraphs 37 and 38. But you appear to nevertheless acknowledge that the municipal authorities were paying the paramilitaries in paragraph 51. You state that Pavlovic, i.e. Popovic, would send us lists for the payment of wages to all the soldiers and paramilitaries as well, these lists were signed by Pavlovic, and we did not dare enter into any more detailed analysis of the people on this list for the reasons already stated. So is it your position that you were suspicious of the names that appeared on Marko Pavlovic's lists but you were too terrified of paramilitaries to ask any questions about them? Is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: First of all, real volunteers reported to the TO staff and then they were deployed. Marko included them among the local fighters in terms of fighting and also in terms of the payroll. And so we did not know who was a local person and who came as a volunteer. Do you understand? It was not written anywhere who was a volunteer and who wasn't a volunteer. Marko signed all the payrolls so when the commander would sign these lists, that was when these payments would be made, or rather, he would send his man to the cashier at the Municipal Assembly and he'd get enough money for a certain number of soldiers per month. And it varied. So we did not have any need to -- and to tell you the truth we didn't dare to single anyone out, even if -- well, no chance, because you -- your head would fly. These were people who were well-versed in warfare. Also, many of them were drunkards, carousers. These were people who did not think much but who were trigger-happy. I didn't ask -- I mean, they took me out for an execution three times, I think. Once they kept me and the entire staff together for hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're starting to repeat things that are in your statement. I just want to make this clear: Is it your evidence that you were too terrified of the paramilitaries to ask any questions about who appeared on these payroll lists? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go to page 159 of the English and page 106 of the B/C/S. I'd like to remind you of what you said before on this topic. So this is at the top of the page in the English and right at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. And you're asked by the Presiding Judge: "Did you discuss those payments with Branko Popovic?" And you said: "No." "For the army for the territorials for the volunteers who had subordinated? And you said: "No, no simply he would present it at the end of a meeting at the meeting." And you're asked: "What would he say in that regard?" And if we turn the page in the B/C/S, you say: "I have this and that many soldiers on the list and I'm asking for this and that many salaries, that is social benefits, so to speak. These were not salaries, they were not taxed or anything, these were simply paid out to people in cash to get through that period until life goes back to normal." And then a few lines down, you're asked: "One TO and everyone under it?" And you say: "Those that he represented and to me he was the one making the requests, the one distributing, and so on. I had full trust in him. " And the judge says: "All right." And then another judge intervenes and he says, this is

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KRSTAJIC
utterances.text: "Mr. Grujic, now I have to ask you a question, you spoke about the problems you were having with this unit, the city was having with this unit, that you yourself were having, and also this government with the members of that unit, for example, you were held there for five hours locked up, and you were almost liquidated?" And you say: "Yes." And then the judge asks: "Then we have to ask you, why did you authorise the payment? Why did you authorise paying out salaries to the members of this unit," and if you turn the page in the English, "and this commander for the month of May when they nearly liquidated you? When you weren't even asking for Karadzic's intervention?" And you said: "As I said, for me, this unit did not exist as a separate unit, for me there was the Territorial Defence as a Territorial Defence." And the judge asks: "Within that frame Pavlovic would submit requests to you even for that unit?" And you say: "I have to be honest again, there was this economy secretary of ours who had a very close relation was this unit. You see, there is even a possibility that he abused his position and that perhaps he made the payment without the government's knowledge" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, please. Objection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is that it is the Prosecutor who is interpreting the words of this witness. They are not being quoted directly. They are being interpreted in a very long question, then you said this and then you said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. She's relying on the transcript from a trial in Belgrade. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you say about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please provide a reference for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S about two-thirds of the way down. It's Branko Grujic's longer answer towards the bottom of the page, about two-thirds of the way down. You're speaking about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Make sure whether we are on the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I did check them all. I believe it's correct. If it's page 107 of the B/C/S then I'm quite confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 32 in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this is -- we could not know the page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, it's the e-court page because there are -- it's -- yeah -- I was just saying that for the Registrar's -- to confirm with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you say there is even a possibility that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Check with the witness he has the correct passage, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you see where you're speaking here, Mr. Grujic? Are you able to follow?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I can see it, and I am aware of all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I can see it myself, in fact, because in the next line the judge refers to the number 10.000 which I can see in the Cyrillic. So you're referring to this economy secretary and you say there is even a possibility that he abused his position and that perhaps he made the payment without the government's knowledge or even without the command's knowledge, I am saying I am not certain that he paid them but there is a great possibility that he did. Now, Mr. Grujic, in your own case, one of the Judges asked you directly why you were paying this unit that you claimed had almost liquidated you, you said nothing about having suspicions about who was on the list but being too afraid to question them, to the contrary you simply responded this unit did not exist as a separate unit. For me there was a Territorial Defence as a Territorial Defence. You also said you had "full trust in Marko Pavlovic in this regard" and you added that a member of your government had a particularly close relationship with this unit. So your evidence now about your government paying these units because they were too terrified to ask any questions is an invention designed to distance yourself and your government at the time from these paramilitaries. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: All of that is correct, that even if we wanted to, we couldn't let them go because I told you a moment ago what kind of people these were and what kind of unit this was and Marko, believe me, always said that they were under his control and that he would take care of them and that he would disband them when he felt that they were not under his control. But he didn't do that for a long time. Now, whether he dared or did not dare, I told you a moment ago he was also once held at gunpoint by them, as I was and the entire staff, so now the question is whether Marko dared intervene because he was trying to preserve his own life too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender these payments, I'd like to add them to P6415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be added.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Grujic, it's true, isn't it, that this economy secretary you referred to and that's Stevo Radic, was particularly close to Zuca and his unit; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: At my trial, a document was shown about the payment of some money to Zuca's unit that had not been signed by Marko Pavlovic and that's when I had my doubts because I did not know this document, I was suspicious in terms of Stevo paying that out without me knowing about it or Marko knowing about it because he often had very close contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. And you said in your own trial that Zuco was often in Stevo Radic's office visiting had him; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 42 of your statement you said that after the paramilitaries were arrested: "Proceedings against all of the RSD's were held before the relevant courts in Republika Srpska and Serbia. The documents support this." Now, the Chamber has received a great deal of evidence that the paramilitaries who were arrested at the end of July were released soon after that. And in fact that's what you said to the OTP in 2002, that they only spent a few days in Bijeljina in prison before being released. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That happened in Bijeljina. That's indeed the way it is, and believe me, I myself was terrified of this situation and this kind of attitude towards people who disturbed the law and order and all the laws of this earth. I was really taken by surprise and I thought that serious proceedings should be initiated against them but that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gustafson said were released soon after that. And what the witness heard was, "freed." And I would prefer to have it interpreted as "released from detention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't follow. She said they were released.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness received an interpretation stating that they were "freed," "oslobodjen," which is different [In English] "acquitted."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think the witness's answer is clear nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grujic at paragraph 71 you assert that the mosque in Zvornik were damaged by the paramilitaries, but in 2002 you told the OTP that the mosques in Zvornik were destroyed by the military unit in Zvornik because they were the ones in possession of the explosives and other materials necessary to carry this out. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No one else could have except for those who had the explosives and it was the volunteers and the regular army who had explosives. Now which one did this I cannot --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you repeat what you said after, "Now which one did this, I cannot," because the interpreters didn't catch the end of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot do any kind of bidding here. I cannot guess whether it was the volunteers or the regular army because they were all there and they all had explosives.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. For my next question, I'd like to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could the Chamber move into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic, you just referred to Arkan and being an eyewitness, and you do make a number of assertions about what happened during the takeover of Zvornik led by Arkan on the 9th of April. But it's right, isn't it, that you didn't participate in the actual takeover operation and you were in Mali Zvornik on the other side of the Drina River while it was ongoing; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 60 of your statement you were shown adjudicated fact 2758 which states that on the 9th of April, 1992, you interrogated and beat an individual who was a protected witness in the Krajisnik case, and the evidence is that that incident took place in the Alhos building sometime later in the day on the 9th of April, 1992. And that's P96, pages 16 and 17, and you state in your statement that because Arkan had fired you, you could not access the prisoners, in response to this adjudicated fact. But it's true that you were in the Alhos building on the afternoon of the 9th of April after the takeover was complete, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I was not there until towards evening. I got there towards evening. And everything that is stated there is a notorious lie. None of that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 24648, pages 57 of the English and 40 of the B/C/S. And this is near the bottom of the page in both languages. Roughly ten lines up from the bottom in the B/C/S, the judge asks you: "Did you go to Alhos on the 9th?" And you said: "Periodically, later, I went in the afternoon when it quieted down." The judge says: "Why?" And you say: "When Radio Zvornik announced that Zvornik was free, and so forth. I went then to Alhos to see what had happened and what the situation was like." If we go to the next page in the B/C/S, you say -- and in English: "And they told me that Arkan's units had routed the Green Berets and that Patriotic League and that they had taken over power in Zvornik." Now, that's true, what you told the Trial Chamber in your own case, you went to Alhos in the afternoon of the 9th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Well, I just told you that it was towards evening. Late afternoon, towards evening, I went for a couple of minutes to see what the situation was, I informed myself a little bit, and then I came back. I didn't dare allow Arkan to find me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if we could go to the next page in the English, and this is about the middle of the page in the B/C/S, the Presiding Judge asks you, and this is at the top in the English: "And when was then Zvornik taken, as you put it? When was this?" And you say: "Well, that didn't last long, it lasted maybe a few hours. Already in the morning. Before at around noon, Radio Zvornik made a broadcast and a Serb presenter spoke, and so on." And you're asked: "And what do they say?" And you answer: "They say that Zvornik is free and that the people should return to their homes, and so on." That's correct, isn't it, that the announcement on Radio Zvornik that the takeover was over and --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- that was around noon. You can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's when the Zvornik blockade was lifted by the Serbian army, when the Green Berets and the Patriotic League left the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm about to move to another topic so if this is a convenient time to take the break, it's certainly convenient for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I'd like to ask you now about the Muslims from Kozluk. At paragraph 69 of your statement you were presented with adjudicated fact 2774, which states among other things that you, Marko Pavlovic and Jovo Mijatovic went to Kozluk on the 26th of June, 1992, and informed the Muslims that they had an hour to leave or they would be killed. And you give a different version of events in your statement, and in your statement you also claim that the Muslims of Kozluk left voluntarily. That's at paragraph 47. We've referred throughout the examination to your trial, the trial against you and Mr. Popovic, and you and Mr. Popovic were ultimately convicted for a number of crimes against Muslims in Zvornik, including the unlawful imprisonment of Muslims from Divic, the unlawful imprisonment of Muslims from the Djulici area, and the forcible displacement of the Muslims from Kozluk. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: It's not correct. First of all, Kozluk left on its own initiative. Nobody went on the 26th out of those mentioned to Kozluk. On the 22nd, but don't hold me to the date, I was called by Peja -- Arkan of -- who said I was in Kozluk with my brother Fadil, they had some problems there, Fadil complained to me, so, please, could you go there to see what happened? Since at that point in time the president of the municipality, Jovo Mijatovic, was in my office I asked him that we go together. We went down there, Fadil told us that somebody was shooting behind the houses, so that the children got frightened, and so on and so forth, and asked us for guarantees. Could we guarantee his freedom and safety? We said we were not in command of the army, that we were unable to command anything, but Arkan's Pejo could guarantee because at that point in time he was in charge of everything, he could things, protect and do whatever else. We went to Arkan's -- we told him to go to Arkan's Pejo, and then see what he said. Arkan's Pejo received only Fadil, he did not even deign to receive us in the office. Later, he informed us that he had agreed with Fadil that people from Kozluk could go to foreign countries but only through Serbia, not through Tuzla or the Federation, which was under the control of the Muslims. So only through Serbia could they go out. And he asked us if we could help, if we could provide transport for him. So whether we wanted to do it or not we had to do it. I think that Jovo Mijatovic again went to see Fadil and agreed the day would be the 26th. And we did provide buses, really, on that day and the escort and everything passed in the best order, peacefully, no one was killed, no one was abused, nothing was done to anyone, everybody went out alive and well and they left for a foreign country as they wished. That is the real truth, that can be spoken. Furthermore, I wanted to ask Madam Prosecutor, you often use my statement before the Trial Chamber as if I testified in court. You are a lawyer, I'm not a lawyer, I did not testify in court. I was defending myself in court or I was testifying to the best of my ability in that court, I did not say an oath, here I did say an oath that I have to speak the truth, but when any kind of legal proceedings are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. No, no. The interpreters didn't catch up with you from where you talked about the oath. Could you repeat from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Prosecutor was using my statement before the Belgrade court as if I was testifying for myself. I did not testify there. There, I was presenting my defence. I have the right to use all available options according to our law that are favourable to me. So please do not compare this with the statement that I am providing here under oath. I would like you to avoid that a little bit, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 25164 and while that's coming up let me just ask you, Mr. Grujic, you said that you draw a distinction between the statement you made in your own trial that we've referred to numerous times where you presented your defence, and the statement you are providing here under oath. So let me ask you, did you tell the truth when you gave a statement in your own trial before the court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I was saying what was in my favour as an accused, that is something that is permissible by law, and here I have to speak the truth because I gave a solemn declaration to speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you're saying that not everything you said when you gave a statement in your own trial, the statement we have been referring to, is true? You told some lies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that I did not speak the whole truth, but according to the law there, I am allowed to use all means available to me regarding the truth. As for whether I spoke the truth or not, that is my personal matter, whether I spoke the truth or not at that trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's clarify this. Ms. Gustafson, you said that he testified in his own trial. Is it that he testified? Do you agree with the witness that he didn't say under oath?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour, under the system that he was operating in, that he presented his defence and he was not under oath. So I -- that's why I was asking the questions I was asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In some civil law jurisdictions the accused are asked by the chamber or by the prosecution or by his defence counsel. That was the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. He was questioned by the judge, the prosecution and his own counsel and I believe it was not under oath, as he states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Grujic, are you not willing the tell the Trial Chamber today whether or not you told the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation. Just a second. Sorry to interrupt you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the way it was written, he says, on page 70, line 23/24: According to our laws, I have the right not to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not say that he lied, but not to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, you said that when I asked you whether you lied when you gave a statement in your own trial, you said, as for whether I spoke the truth or not, that is my personal matter. Are you saying that you're not willing to tell the Trial Chamber today even though those proceedings against you are completed, whether or not you told the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I'm not obliged to do that and I have the right to keep that to myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This document in front of you, Mr. Grujic, is the judgement against you and the first part is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm -- just a second. I didn't follow the previous question and answer. What was the question? Are you saying that you are not willing to tell the Trial Chamber today? Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him whether it was correct that he was not willing to tell Your Honours whether or not his statement in his own trial was true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understand the question. But you made the solemn declaration, Mr. Grujic, today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did make the statement, and I will be speaking the truth about events. As for my conduct before the chamber in Belgrade, in that court, I do not wish to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no in that court -- [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's deal with it when a specific issue arises with respect to a specific statement. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, this is the appeals judgement against you and if we go to page 2 of the English and remaining on page 1 in the B/C/S, it states that the judgement, trial judgement against you, was upheld. And that's correct, isn't it? Your appeal was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is this document confidential?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, it is not, not to my knowledge. I believe it's a public judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is indicated in e-court that it is confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand why, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This -- I can explain it. Maybe we should move briefly in private session. I don't think it needs to remain such, but perhaps the explanation in private session will be simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session, briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grujic, the trial judgement was upheld by the appeals chamber, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in the English and page 54 in the B/C/S, to the beginning of the trial judgement, you see that this is the beginning of the judgement, your name appears as an accused, if we could go to the next page in both languages, and it refers to Branko Popovic's name and it says -- the heading says: Are guilty. And on the next page, it summarises the guilty verdict taking hostage Muslims 174 persons from the village of Divic, taking hostage around 700 persons from the village of Djulici, Klisa and other settlements and on the 26th of June forcibly displacing the Muslim population of Kozluk. If we could just scroll through the next several pages until we get to page 10 of the English and page 59 of the B/C/S, where the Court summarises its findings with respect to these three sets of crimes. And on page 10 of the English and page 59 of the B/C/S, and this starts at the very bottom of the page in the B/C/S. And near the top in the English, it states that the respective accused went to Kozluk, the accused Popovic to the Kozluk Crisis Staff on the eve of the day of departure while the accused Grujic and Jovo Mijatovic went to the police station on the day of the departure. If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, it says where through a member of the police the accused Grujic invites the president of Kozluk local commune to the police station, Fadil Banjanovic, whom he verbally orders to call all the inhabitants of Muslim ethnicity to prepare on short notice to leave the village of Kozluk and move out via the Republic of Serbia towards other countries, following which Mijatovic informed the aggrieved party in the form of an ultimatum that they were surrounded and that they had to move out threatening that they would all be killed, otherwise that the remark of the aggrieved party Banjanovic that they do not have any transportation means, the accused Grujic informed Banjanovic that the buses and trucks had already been provided. You said that none of you, Pavlovic or Mijatovic, were in Kozluk on the 26th of June, but it's clear that the Trial Chamber found that you were. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: This is not right. The Trial Chamber unfortunately believed Fadil Banjanovic who was a false witness who said on day one that we had come on the 26th, he mentioned some 3.000 soldiers who were expelling people from their houses by force, et cetera. However, the same witness, the false witness, said literally the following on the next day. We stalled with our departure because we had some 50 or 60 people who did not want to join us so we had to pull them out, literally, from their houses to join us. Then I asked the Prosecutor who was it who drove those people by force, whether it was myself or Mr. Banjanovic, and the Chamber ruled based on his testimony on the first day, because they wanted to convict me at any cost. The treacherous regime in the Serbia at the time, and Mr. Tadic needed this conviction in order for him to be able to go around Bosnia, offer apologies and boast about court decisions, whereas, in fact, the court convicted an innocent person. I behaved in my municipality in the manner that I tried to protect every resident, but unfortunately the politicians of Serbia needed that at the time and they acted accordingly and as a result they passed judgement as they wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is missing in line 6 is "around Brussels and in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is kindly asked to wait for interpretation to finish before intervening. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, usual request from the interpreters to wait for the interpretation to finish before the intervention, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, at paragraph 47 of your statement you said that the inhabitants of Kozluk themselves initiated their moving out because they felt unsafe due to the battlefield being nearby. And again you made the same claim in your defence at your trial but the court in your case rejected that argument as well on the basis that the line of separation was far away from the village, there was no fighting in the village, Kozluk and its immediate surroundings were inside Serb-controlled territory and that the Serb forces carried out staged attacks to try to make it look like the departure was voluntary. And perhaps we should go to those passages, I can show them to you, and if you want to comment you can. If we go to page 42 of the English, page 214 of the B/C/S, this is at the bottom in the English and at the very top in the B/C/S. It says, however, as was stated above, the court has established in a manner that is beyond doubt that the safety of the inhabitants of Kozluk was not in danger in the manner in which the accused Grujic presents it because the line of separation was far away and because there was no fighting in Kozluk itself which the accused are not denying either, and that the attacks on Kozluk were staged by the Serb side to the conflict. And at page 45 of the English, page 218 of the B/C/S, the Court goes into this in more detail, stating that the defence was that the claim that the moving away was a result of the free decision by the Kozluk residents and the Court concludes that the forcible transfer of Kozluk residents was not justified either -- by either reasons of the population security nor by imperative military reasons, states that the TO had organised the handing over of -- and this is the next page in the B/C/S -- handing over of the Kozluk residents' weapons long before the departure. There was no fighting in Kozluk. Kozluk locals did not represent a military threat. On the next page in the English it points out that the line of separation was 6 kilometres from Kozluk and the immediate surroundings were under the control of the Serb side. The court says one cannot deny that the population was scared which is completely logical but forcible transfer could in no event have been an alternative to offering the population every sort of assistance to stay on in their homes. And in the next paragraph, about halfway down, the court says, the court has established that in this concrete case, this force in terms of the expulsion is also reflected in the artificial creation of an unbearable situation that was supposed to result in the conclusion that they had moved away voluntarily which was not the case. Now, that's correct, isn't it, Mr. Grujic? These people did not move away because, as you said, the battlefield was nearby. This was an organised, planned expulsion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: None of this is true that a separation line was less than 3 kilometres. Shells even fell in Serbia. They flew over Kozluk to Banja Koviljaca to Mali Zvornik, there was even a casualty in Mali Zvornik from a shell that came from the separation line. Now, how can anyone say that they were not threatened by the proximity of the battlefield? In such close proximity, 2 to 3 kilometres, people were using their -- losing their brothers and fathers and other relatives. People were afraid to walk around the area and nobody could guarantee that a person would grab a rifle and go to avenge the deaths of their relatives. Many of the inhabitants of Kozluk crossed over to the enemy side and were fighting our troops, and we could not risk anyone going mad and taking to weapons and killing people's randomly. Both the judges in Belgrade and you here are overlooking the situation that in early May Kozluk, Gornji, Sekapa [phoen] and Sotici [phoen] set off on their own towards Tuzla. All of them gathered together in one place, in cars and other vehicles, but Arkan's Pejo didn't allow them to travel towards Tuzla because they said they will get hold of rifles there and they will turn against them. Instead he said that he would guarantee them safety and eventually an agreement was reached and all of them returned home. After Arkan's Pejo gave his word, the archbishop came --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, could you speak more slowly? Could you repeat from where you said, "Arkan's Pejo gave his word ..." Start from "archbishop ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. [Interpretation] It's a mistake. He did not say that after Pejo gave his word the bishop came, and the witness can explain when the bishop actually came. It is nothing to do with giving the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when those three villages set off of their own volition, nobody was forcing them, and they all assembled in Kozluk in cars, in lorries, and other vehicles available, and virtually nearly all of them were on the road. Arkan's Pejo did not allow them to pass through towards Tuzla. Instead, he called our bishop and the "hodza" from Tuzla. They both came to speak to the people and persuade them not to leave, then he was going to guarantee their safety in their own homes. People abided by this plea and went back to their houses. Kozluk used to have 5.000 inhabitants; 1459 of them, if I remember correctly, left on the 26th of June. Now, where were the two-thirds? They had left earlier and they were in third countries and they were calling upon those who remained behind to join them and not to remain there where there was shelling on a daily basis and shooting every day. This is what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, the interpreters are not able to catch up with your speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I become agitated and excited and therefore I make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender the pages that I've referred to. It's pages 1 to 11, 42 to 46 in the English, and pages 154 to 60 and 214 to 219 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to -- we don't have any objection to the pages that the witness has actually commented on being admissible for purposes of assessing his credibility, but inasmuch as you normally admit documents for all purposes, I want to point out that any findings of this Court would not be admissible for any other purpose other than this witness's credibility, in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, do you disagree with Mr. Robinson's statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. These judgements have been coming in with various witnesses for various purposes. This is the first I've heard of this being relevant only to credibility. I think the finding of another chamber beyond a reasonable doubt in a criminal trial upheld on appeal is certainly relevant for this Trial Chamber to consider for matters going beyond credibility. Of course, it's always up to this Trial Chamber to reach its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you admit the Galic judgement or other judgements, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact there was a previous request to tender pages of the Martic judgement with Mr. Martic, and Mr. Robinson stated that the Trial Chamber could take judicial notice of that so there was no need to tender it, and on that bases we declined to do so. But again there was no reference to this being relevant only to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the speed in which you should proceed. French translation has been just now concluded. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's our position that Rule 94 is lex specialis for the taking of judicial notice of adjudicated facts from other judgements and that in that rule does not allow for adjudicated facts to be taken for judgements in other jurisdictions other than this Tribunal. So then by taking those facts that are found in other judgements as -- other than for credibility, would be outside of that lex specialis and improper, in our view. One thing I've noticed in the other judgements that we have admitted, we have basically been admitting the verdict, not the reasoning. In this particular judgement the verdict and the reasoning are all mixed in, and so we are admitting portions of the reasoning, and that's why I thought it was particularly important to bring it up in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the Chamber has ever admitted a judgement of other trial chamber or other jurisdiction for the facts contained in the judgement. We will admit it for credibility issue. Shall we assign the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tendered pages of document 25164 receives number P6416, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, in the last paragraph on this page, the court referred to evidence that the decision to move out the Muslims of Kozluk was a matter of higher politics, and the Court concluded that higher authorities relative to you and Mr. Popovic were certainly involved but that did not affect your own responsibility, and it's true, isn't it, that higher authorities were involved in this? And in particular, Dr. Karadzic was involved in this decision to move the Muslims out of Kozluk and settle Serbs there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic never said a word about the Muslims of Kozluk or about any moving out. He even never allowed us to forcibly relocate someone, God for bid. We did it on our own because we assessed the situation was such that people were willing to leave voluntarily, in order to save their children and their family. And we did it in order to avoid that, God forbid, Zuco or some other raided Kozluk and committed various things. In fact, I was convicted for not protecting people, but in fact I was unable to provide protection for them. I believe that it would be less painful for those people to allow to go to a safe territory and save their families until such time as the situation became calmer and, thank God, after the war the situation changed and all these people came back and resettled again in Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have P1478, please, page 246 of the English and page 244 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, this is an extract from General Mladic's military notebook on the 30th of June, 1992, reflecting a meeting held in Zvornik attended by Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. We already discussed the existence of this meeting in a document we dealt with in private session. And if we go to the next page, we can see that you are listed as being present, as well as Mr. Pavlovic. And if we could go to page 249 of the English and page 246 of the B/C/S -- I'm sorry, page 247, and under number 4 at the bottom - should be page 249 of the English, please - there is you listed as speaking and you state according to these notes, we have 32.000 Serbs, and then you state we have successfully implemented the president's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children. And the words "with our children" appear on the next page so we should go to the next page to see the end there. Now, this is just four days after the Muslims of Kozluk had been moved out. And when you say we have successfully implemented the president's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children, you're referring to President Karadzic and his decision, aren't you? That's the president you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can I see the next page? This doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said so, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is probably an abbreviation provided by the general. I don't know what he had in mind. A moment ago I told you that Arkan's Pejo turned people back when they wanted to leave Kozluk, that he had guaranteed safety for them. I never uttered these words and I never mentioned President Karadzic at this meeting and in this context. If Mr. Mladic really wrote this he was either drunk or he didn't hear well, and he was often partial to good drink and he may have been mistaken. And I'm telling you none of the things that are written here are true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 251 of the English and page 249 of the B/C/S, and here Mr. Pavlovic is speaking, and if we could go to page 253 of the English and page 251 of the B/C/S, this is still Mr. Pavlovic speaking, and right at the bottom he says, and this goes over to the next page: "We were most active in evicting the Muslims. We had brought peace to Sepak, Divic and Kozluk. Some of them wanted" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He says: "We were most active in evict being the Muslims. We had brought peace to Sepak, Divic and Kozluk." If we could go to the next page: "Some of them wanted to move out while we demanded it, we had to evict some of the people also for the sake of our 'heroes who fled from Kovacevici.'" We need the next page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, please, we've already had this discussion about the word "evicting." It's not that, it's "moving."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. If he wants to request an official revision of this translation, we may have already been through this before, then he can. But this is not the appropriate time to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Chamber notes the issue. Shall we continue, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, a moment ago you said that Dr. Karadzic never said a word about the Muslims of Kozluk or about anyone moving out, he even never allowed to us forcibly relocate someone, God forbid. But here, Mr. Pavlovic is expressly reporting to President Karadzic and General Mladic that the Zvornik authorities have been actively evicting Muslims including those from Kozluk, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that Mr. Popovic ever uttered these words. This can be some kind of mistake or forgery. I never heard this. Believe me. As far as Radovan Karadzic is concerned, he always said to us that in our territory, and I've already said this, we even have to give them privileges, these other ethnic communities, not harm them in any way, heaven forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 270 of the English, page 268 of the B/C/S, there was much discussion in this meeting about Captain Dragan's training centre and we can see here Dr. Karadzic says, it would be a shame to abolish the centre. It would be easiest for us to put the incident behind us. The men at the centre are not like Zuca and Crni. Now, at paragraphs 40 and 41 of your statement, Mr. Grujic, you assert that following your unpleasant contacts with Zuco in the beginning of July, you and Marinko Vasilic secretly went to Pale to inform President Karadzic about the problems of paramilitaries in Zvornik and you state that President Karadzic was "visibly surprised and astonished by what I had told him." Now, your evidence does not make sense for two reasons: First, Dr. Karadzic was clearly in Zvornik on the 30th of June hearing about problems with paramilitaries, so it doesn't make sense that a week or so later you went to Pale to inform him about the problems that he'd just heard about in Zvornik; and secondly, your evidence that he was visibly surprised and astonished by your report doesn't square with the notes of this meeting indicating that he was hearing all about problems with paramilitaries; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, you either were not listening or you do not want to accept what I said. I told you clearly that on the 13th we had not had any information about what was going on in Celopek, and so on. And already on the 1st of July we did have information. And now I cannot say to him on the 1st of June what I knew, or rather, on the 30th what I found out on the 1st of July. Well, that is why Mr. Karadzic was not informed on the 30th. That's why he was informed later when we were already compelled -- I mean, I informed the organs of Serbia since they were not doing anything, the situation got more difficult and continued to be difficult, and therefore we had to go to see Mr. Karadzic and tell him, Mr. President, I cannot take it down there anymore, the commander cannot set up the army and place it under his command, they are almost stronger than the rest of the TO. The police 30, 40, I don't know how many of them there were, they -- there were so few of them and that's why the chief of police and I went to President Karadzic to resolve this matter personally with his own authority and influence, and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, the truth is that you and Mr. Vasilic did go to Pale to meet with Dr. Karadzic, but you in fact went to Pale in May, not July, and at that meeting Dr. Karadzic was not visibly surprised and astonished by what you told him; to the contrary, he said he knew all about Zuco already and Zuco was his problem.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Not true. Not in May. We were there in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25264, page 77 in the English and page 74 of the B/C/S. Now, this is the interview you gave to the OTP in 2002, again, and I'd like to direct your attention to the middle of the page in the B/C/S, this is towards the bottom in the English -- or sorry, yes, it's at the bottom of the B/C/S as well, and you're asked I have to say a point of extraordinary that before the war so much effort was put in by you and others to create an environment where there would be a rule of law in case of an emergency of some sort and then when that effectively occurred, and if we go to the next page in the B/C/S, that is to say that the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, but I cannot find what you are reading out now. Down there; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. This is the question you're asked at the bottom of the page, and the question continues on the next page, and you're asked that is to say that there were general acts of lawlessness that you directly observed yourself and you took no action to stop it. And then you see your answer near the top of the page there. You say, as a matter of fact, as you told you, Dragan was there and charged for -- in charge for this couple of critical days upon which we asked Marko to intervene with Arkan and did so, I repeatedly had to ask Arkan to introduce some order, however these people were ordinary villains and ex-prisoners, drug addicts, stuff like that. And then the next page in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the B/C/S I can't find the word "Dragan" at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It may have been a mis -- it is the correct passage. It might have been just a mistake in the interpretation. We didn't have a single soldier, policeman, who could oppose them, who could stand up against them. Then you're asked but as the president of the original government after the 10th or 12th or whatever it was, was it incumbent on you to make sure that they housed the municipal SDS, the municipal, the Bosnian Serbs at Pale or wherever --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please provide the reference for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the question that begins PB, about a third of the way down the page. Were made aware that such lawlessness had taken hold in Zvornik. And then you answer in the middle of the page, As a matter of facts I did go to Radovan at one point together with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters think that this is not the correct page in the B/C/S. We are talking about the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It should be page 75 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That cannot be seen in Serbian. There is only one sentence at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the correct part in the B/C/S but it may be broken up differently. I just ask the interpreters to try their best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably there are many inaudible parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That may be correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you say, As a matter of fact I did it go to Radovan at one point together with the head of TO staff Marinko Vasilic and I told him that I would give up the office and leave everything if they don't help us and indeed subsequently he sent a special unit of MUP and they have arrested those people. And you were asked at the bottom of the page, When did you report this to Karadzic? And on the next page in the B/C/S, you say, I don't know the exact date but I remember on that very day the army was leaving, the JNA was leaving, the Tito's military [indiscernible] in Sarajevo. I was in Pale on that very day with Radovan, with President Karadzic. Now, Mr. Grujic, it's common ground that the JNA pulled out around the 20th of May, 1992, and you specifically remembered that event as being the day that you and Mr. Vasilic met with Dr. Karadzic in Pale, so that's correct, isn't it? You actually went to Pale towards the end of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true. Possibly I went to Pale then for some other meeting. And, you know, there are documents about the arrest of this unit at the end of July and we were there a few days before that, I and Marinko. Maybe I made a mistake when I made my statement, but please do check. This unit was arrested at the end of July. I don't know the exact date. And we were there two or three days before that, and the president said that he would resolve that immediately so he just needed two or three days to provide the right units for the arrest of those persons so that must be a mistake. We were there in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would ask to add these two pages to P6414 and if we go to page 144 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will do so but how much more do you need, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can complete within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 144 in the English. There is no -- there is no B/C/S transcript in existence for this passage. And here you're asked again about your efforts or lack of efforts to bring the paramilitaries into order and you're asked near the top of the page, Can you tell us why you didn't turn to the JNA as an available source to try to bring these men into order? And you say, So there was a very small JNA, Obrenovic's unit, with a couple of tanks and only 20 to 30 men there, whereas the paramilitaries were stronger than anybody else. These were the notorious fighters that came from Croatia, there were also ex-prisoners among them, and this is why again I couldn't complain to the TO commander because he was also there with a gun pointed at his head. And that is why I went directly along with the head of the SUP of the police to the president, Radovan Karadzic, and I told him I'll resign, I'll demand to be released from the duty, and he said, don't you worry, I heard about these incidents, and I will sort them out urgently, and upon which the action of the special unit, and the remainder is inaudible. So, Mr. Grujic, the truth is that when you went to Pale to complain to Dr. Karadzic about the paramilitaries, he was not visibly surprised and astonished, as you assert in your statement, but, rather, he said he'd already heard about these incidents; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: No, no. I heard, that's what he says. That means that he heard it from me. So that means that he accepts what I said to him at that moment. That is to say I take note of these problems. I heard, that means that he heard it then. Had he heard about it earlier on, he certainly would have done something about it so that this would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's see what you said in your own trial about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page as well to be added to P6414 and I'd like to go to 65 ter 24648, page 125 of the English and page 85 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of this witness's evidence, you will upload only those pages admitted and that also may be -- that may also be admitted during the course of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is towards the bottom of the page, Mr. Grujic, in the B/C/S where you give a relatively long answer starting about 15 lines up from the bottom. It's also near the bottom in the English. And in about the third sentence of your answer you say, However, during the month of June, there were again frequent, so to say, to put it that way, robberies, provocations, firing guns in the town and so on and so on. Therefore they cause havoc again. At one moment I asked the commander this chief of the SUP, Mr. Vasilic, Chief, can you are you capable of restraining these people, preventing this from happening again? He told me, listen, and then you are interrupted and the judge says, Preventing what from happening? And you say, Preventing those provocations from happening so that the town could be quiet for once. There would be no guns firing in the town, no break-ins, no robberies and so on. This is the next page in the English, he said, Listen, I do not have such a policeman. The judge asked, This Marinko, you say, Yes, I do not have such a policeman who would fire at a Serb, a volunteer, be sure of that. What are we to do? He said, I do not know, and then proposed that we go and see president Radovan Karadzic. And then you talk about the road being opened. And you say, So we went to see Radovan Karadzic, and you say, I informed him about the whole situation about what was happening, Radovan said, I have already heard many things about that Zuca. I told him, President, I am not returning to Zvornik, I will not go to the town unless you resolve this situation. And you're asked, Was that the first time you went to see Dr. Karadzic? And you say, The first time, yes, it was. And you -- you're asked, When was that? You say, I do not know. Believe me it was sometimes towards the end of June on the 20th and something June thereabouts. I told him I will not return to Zvornik ever again, that if needs be I will escape Republika Srpska entirely. He said, I have heard about that Zuca. I know all about it. Go and do your job. Zuca is my responsibility. You said it twice here, Mr. Grujic. Although you changed your story slightly and you said this was in June rather than May, as you told the OTP. You said twice that Dr. Karadzic knew all about Zuca and that Zuca was his responsibility. He was not visibly surprised and astonished by what you told him, was he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Madam, you have the wrong translation there. I have already explained that to you. That is to say Radovan said I heard all of that from you now, I take note of all of that, that is my concern, I'm going to resolve it as soon as possible, so that is not a correct translation. Radovan never said to me that he had heard about it earlier on. He said that he heard about it from me and that he took note of that. So, please, do not use something that is not right, actually maybe you're reading something that was mistranslated so that's why I ask you kindly, well, further on, find the document, when the fighters were arrested, at the end of July, that is to say that we were there a few days before that, a day or two before they were arrested and that was in the month of July. It's not May, it's not June, it's July. Please. And don't keep insisting on these dates. It's been more than 20 years now. I'm an old man and please stop insisting on dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would seek to add these two pages to P6415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I have one last document to show you, Mr. Grujic, it's 65 ter 25294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, apologies. It's pages 125 and 126 of the English and -- sorry, the 65 ter number, it's 25294, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, the document that's about to come up on your screen is a "New York Times" article from the 7th of March, 1994, and it describes an interview you gave to a "New York Times" reporter around that time where you showed him a church you were building on a cliff overlooking Zvornik. First, I'd like to ask you: Do you recall giving an interview to an English speaking reporter around that time and showing him the church?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but journalists came to see me several times and I gave several interviews. Which one this was I cannot remember exactly and I cannot say whether that is that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. This is in English so I'll read some parts out to you and maybe it will remind you. In the third paragraph it states arriving at last at the summit of the cliff Grujic paused to kiss a wooden cross he has had erected before declaring, "The Turks destroyed the Serbian church that was here when they arrived in Zvornik in 1463. Now we are rebuilding the church and reclaiming this as Serbian land forever and ever." Do you recall stating something along those lines on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Possibly. At Kula Grad? It's mentioned way back in 1410. The Serbian despot Stevan. I mean, actually it was Djuradj, he built a tower up there and then later on there was a church. When the Turks came, real Turks, not these Muslims, when they came in 14-something, when they really came to Bosnia, then they destroyed it. I said Turks. I didn't say Muslims. Possibly, that's the way it was, and indeed later on we built a church there, and to this day there is a church up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. About halfway down the page, little bit further down, you're quoted as saying, look at the bell tower, and pointing to the bell tower on this church you're constructing. And then stating, "I am praying to God to give President Clinton the wisdom to abandon the Muslims and return to his true allies, the Christians." Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's a mistranslation. No church tower was there. There was no church. There was just this wooden cross at the place where the church used to be. All of that is written incorrectly and I do not accept that as a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, in the second paragraph, it states that the Bosnian government wants Zvornik back if a peace settlement is to be reached and it says this notion makes Grujic laugh. "Return to Zvornik," the mayor scoffed, "the Muslims must be joking. This was a Serbian town before Islam existed in the Balkans. They better not dream of things they cannot fulfil or things will just get worse. Either a peace is worked out soon or we Serbs advance. We cannot stand still, Kalesija is Muslim now but it may not be for long." Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I said that, and even if I did, this was a time of war, a time of euphoria so it's no wonder that I said something like that but I really don't recall saying something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And towards the bottom of the page, it states that the mayor looked down at the deserted formerly Muslim you village of Divic on a lip of land on the Drina and announced that he had renamed it Sveti Stevan after the Christian Saint Stevan. Then he turned to the devastated expanse behind him called Kula hill and said, it would be renamed Djuradj hill after Djuradj Brankovic, the medieval Serbian ruler who built the first church on this site in 1410. Now a moment ago you actually spontaneously referred to this person -- Djuradj built the church in 1400, so I assume you acknowledge that you stated that to this report on this occasion as well. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: This was not something spontaneous. Even today it's called Djurdjev Grad, Djurdjev town. Our municipality changed the name, so it's not anything unusual. As for Divic, I don't know what date it was, Divic was not destroyed, not a single house was damaged. All the houses that were there before the war are still standing there today. Therefore, these are either tendentious assertions or the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It doesn't say that it was destroyed, it says it was deserted, and it states that you announced you would rename --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: You said destroyed. You said destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation said that, "unisten," "destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you talked about renaming Divic Sveti Stevan after the Christian Saint Stevan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that. That was definitely not said. That was fabricated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25294 receives number P6417, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, I believe that we might have to spill over into tomorrow and I'm going to use the ten minutes or so that are left for today's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grujic, earlier you said, this is maybe on page 69 or 70, and then you repeated it again on page 80 but it was not recorded that Fadil Banjanovic needed to prove himself in Sarajevo and Tadic needed to prove that he was bringing to court, and before that you said the traitorous regime in Serbia then had the need to bring people to trial. Can you please tell us why that was so, in the briefest possible way, why do you think that they needed judgements?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: In my personal opinion, these were servants of America, they listened to Washington more than their own people, and they did everything for the benefit of America and nothing for the benefit of Serbia and the Serbian people. They were trying to prove themselves in Europe, all for the sake of some sort of entry into the European Union or getting some sort of date. He was capable of doing anything just to prove that he was doing something. That was the reason. And as for -- just one more thing. As for Fadil Banjanovic, this came out. Later, he was given some posts as a minister, the man is completely illiterate, but he was given the office of minister, he profited well for launching the charges against Arkan and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this Prosecution show any interest in you and in your conduct during the war? Did you have any meetings or interviews and how were you treated, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Which Prosecutor's office and when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I was interviewed in 2002, that was the first time I had contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who interviewed you, what did they say, and what capacity was it in, as a witness or a potential --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: As a suspect. I was interviewed but since they saw that they did not have enough proof they abandoned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which prosecutor was working on it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Well, really, believe me, I don't know. There are documents so you can find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have that document in Belgrade from this Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at 1D25842 in e-court, please. Can we now look at the following page, please. This is the rules of the road, recommendation, your name, 4th of July, 2000, crime alleged, [In English] Initiating and organising the ethnic cleansing of Zvornik. Recommendation B, evidence is insufficient. [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little bit so that we can look at the third paragraph, please. And at the end it says Fadil Banjanovic. Now we will see what he says: [In English] "After the population was put onto trucks, Grujic wanted the able-bodied men to be separated but after the witness refused, he gave up." [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page. So this Prosecution interviewed Banjanovic, Pasic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: I was interviewed in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it says here Mirsad Hasanovic [In English] "Not clear whether he was beaten by Grujic or if Grujic even knew what was going to happen." [Interpretation] And finally the conclusion is [In English] "Under accepted international standards there is insufficient evidence establishing reasonable grounds to believe that Branko Grujic committed serious violations of international humanitarian law." [Interpretation] Did the Court in Belgrade have access to this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC
utterances.text: It did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender these three pages, the cover page and these two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
